books.section: Topic 6.6 The Rise of Industrial Capitalism
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company (1904)

options.misconception: Tarbell stresses enormous profits, not losses.
options.text: That it lost money every year
That its profits and dividends were enormous

options.misconception: Standard Oil was a private company, not a government firm.
options.text: That it was owned by the federal government

options.misconception: Tarbell says nothing about how many workers the company employed.
options.text: That it employed very few workers

rationales.A: Tarbell says the company makes far more than it pays out, and carries an ample reserve fund.
rationales.B: Tarbell opens with the company’s enormous profits and counts dividends of about forty-five million dollars a year.
rationales.C: Background: Standard Oil was Rockefeller’s private company. The government investigated it; it did not own it.
rationales.D: The passage is about profits and dividends, not about the size of the workforce.
rationales.general:
Start with Tarbell’s first sentence.
1. Her first sentence calls the company’s profits enormous.
2. She then counts them: about forty-five million dollars a year in dividends.
3. She adds that the company keeps a reserve fund besides.
4. The whole passage is a count of how much money the combination made.
Remember: an author’s first sentence usually names what the passage is about.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)
stem: What does Tarbell emphasize about the Standard Oil Company?

stimulus.source_note: Ida M. Tarbell, The History of the Standard Oil Company, Vol. 2, Chapter 18 (1904), public domain.
stimulus.text: “The profits of the present Standard Oil Company are enormous. For five years the dividends have been averaging about forty-five million dollars a year, or nearly fifty per cent. on its capitalisation, a sum which capitalised at five per cent. would give $900,000,000. Of course this is not all that the combination makes in a year. It allows an annual average of 5.77 per cent. for deficit, and it carries always an ample reserve fund.”
